bull_bear.body: 100% capex funded by internal accruals; net debt reduction priority (target: net debt-free in 12 months); no external fundraising; dividends expected within FY25 after compliance resolution; no share buybacks mentioned
bull_bear.title: Capital allocation

bull_bear.body: Coking coal price volatility (import-dependent); execution delays in blast furnace revamp (Q1FY26); potential regulatory delays in environmental clearances; competition from PVC/OPVC in municipal water projects (though management dismisses threat); global steel demand slowdown impacting ferro alloy prices
bull_bear.title: Risks & watch-items

bull_bear.body: Highly confident, bullish, and execution-focused; repeated emphasis on ROE/ROC >40%, net debt-free target, and demand-supply imbalance in DI pipes; dismissive of competition and PVC threats; transparent on capex and margins; proactive on investor communication
bull_bear.title: Management quality / tone

bull_bear.body: Captive sinter production (12lakh tons) is a hidden cost advantage — replaces expensive iron ore/pellets; waste heat boiler (35TPH) will reduce grid power dependence and carbon footprint — not yet priced into valuation; 30% ferro alloy output is captive for DI production — vertical integration reduces external procurement risk
bull_bear.title: Non-obvious takeaways

bull_bear.body:
- Sustained focus on Net Term Debt reduction; FY26 Net Term Debt-to-Equity stood at a healthy 0.07x, giving ample headroom for future growth.
- Net Term Debt has fallen sharply from Rs. 3,408 Cr (FY21) to Rs. 188 Cr (Q1FY27); the company has also been sanctioned a Working Capital Loan of Rs. 425 Cr.
- Capex (Rs. 1,076 Cr spent so far) has been funded mostly through internal accruals, reflecting strong internal cash generation and funding capability.
bull_bear.title: Capital allocation policy (investor deck)

bull_bear.body:
- Integrated manufacturing architecture participating across multiple stages of the value chain, giving greater control over critical inputs, production processes and costs, and reducing dependence on external market conditions
- Product diversification across ferro alloys, pig iron, TMT bars, billets and DI pipes, giving the flexibility to shift product mix towards products where opportunities are relatively stronger
- Captive power giving greater control over an important element of manufacturing cost, plus three dedicated railway sidings supporting logistics efficiency
- Proximity to iron ore sources and railway sidings strengthening raw material security and cost competitiveness
- Specialised ferro alloys portfolio supported by long-term customer relationships and premium realisations
- Process initiatives such as sinter recycling and pulverised coal injection that reduce metallurgical coke consumption and optimise hot metal costs
- Ability to produce both steel-grade and foundry-grade pig iron, reducing dependence on a single market
- Dual-channel distribution in TMT bars combining a dedicated project sales team for government and semi-government projects with a dealer network, dealer schemes and channel incentives, achieved without dependence on high-cost celebrity endorsements
- Deleveraged balance sheet described by management as a strategic asset, with high-cost debt reduced and interest rates renegotiated
- External recognition through the ICC Technology Excellence Award 2026 for Sustainability Excellence and the 19th Exceed Environment Award 2025 in the Legend (Emerging) category
bull_bear.title: Bull — competitive strengths

bull_bear.body:
- Coking coal import dependence and volatile raw-material cost — India lacks sufficient high-quality coking coal for blast-furnace steelmaking, so producers rely heavily on imports from countries such as Australia, exposing them to supply disruption, freight cost increases and global price volatility. The BRSR material-issues table separately flags raw material availability and supply fluctuations as a risk with negative implications for procurement cost and production schedules.
- Low-priced imports, Chinese oversupply and dumping — Management states the steel industry operated in a challenging global environment marked by subdued international steel prices and persistent pressure from low-priced imports, particularly from China. The MD&A SWOT names China becoming a net exporter and dumping by competitors as threats that depress domestic prices and compress margins.
- DI pipe demand dependent on government tendering and funding — The DI pipe business is closely linked to public spending on water infrastructure; during FY 2025-26 delays in government ordering, funding availability and project implementation reduced demand visibility, constrained capacity utilisation and intensified pricing competition. This is a structural concentration on a single, policy-driven buyer channel.
- Energy intensity and rising energy costs — BRSR material issue 1: iron and steel manufacturing is highly energy-intensive, making energy efficiency and energy management important to controlling operating costs; the stated financial implication is negative through increased production costs.
- Environmental clearance and permitting delays on expansion — BRSR material issue 3: stricter environmental clearances and permitting requirements may delay expansion or new projects, with a negative implication of increased project costs. This is material given two expansion-cum-modification proposals for Unit 1 and Unit 3 were under environmental assessment during the year.
- Cyclical demand and commodity price exposure — BRSR material issue 4 flags fluctuations in demand due to economic cycles impacting sales volumes and revenue. The Chairman notes commodity businesses are inherently exposed to market cycles, with prices moving on global supply-demand balances, raw material costs and capacity additions, producing a higher degree of earnings volatility.
- Workforce attrition and skilled-labour shortage — BRSR material issue 6 flags that shortages of skilled labour can hinder productivity, quality and innovation. The BRSR turnover table shows permanent-worker turnover rose sharply in FY 2025-26 versus the prior year, making retention a live operational concern.
- Currency and trade-policy exposure on exports — BRSR material issue 9 flags currency fluctuations and changes in trade policies affecting costs, revenues and market access. The Company exports to approximately 32 countries and the BRSR states exports contribute 5.88% of total turnover, while the MD&A names protectionism in Western markets as a threat restricting access to export markets.

business.body:
- One of the largest manufacturers of value-added products (DI Pipes & Specialized Ferro Alloys) in the private sector in Eastern India, with 5 manufacturing units across West Bengal & Chhattisgarh and 1.1 MT of integrated greenfield steel manufacturing.
- "Jai Balaji 2.0" strategy centers on DI Pipes, Specialized Ferro Alloys and other value-added products combined with a strong balance sheet, aiming to transition JBIL into a high-margin company.
- One of the largest producers of Specialized Ferro Alloys in India, with 3 Star Export House Status and export presence in 40+ countries.
business.title: Positioning (investor deck)

business.body:
- [Government Policy Tailwind] Jal Jeevan Mission 2.0 (outlay ₹8.69 lakh Cr, extended to Dec 2028), AMRUT 2.0 (outlay ₹2.99 lakh Cr) and river-interlinking projects (e.g., Ken-Betwa ₹44,605 Cr, Polavaram + Godavari-Krishna Link) underpin a medium-to-long-term demand pipeline for the DI Pipes segment as government order flows normalize.
- [SWOT] Strengths: fully integrated steel company, diversified product range, experienced leadership, lowest cost of capex. Weakness: delayed capacity benefits. Opportunities: strengthening Special Grade Ferro Alloys market, JJM 2.0/Amrut Sarovar-driven DI Pipes demand, government infrastructure push, growth in Railways/Logistics. Threats: ongoing inflation, geopolitical instability, commodity price volatility.
- [Shareholding] Promoter & Promoter Group held 64.84% as on 30 June 2026, with Public (Domestic Institutions 0.10%, FPIs 2.78%, Non-Institutions 32.27%) holding the balance.
business.title: Notable from the deck

business.body: The Company runs an integrated steel plant and manufactures metal and metal products, deriving effectively all of its turnover from manufacturing. Its portfolio spans specialised ferro alloys, pig iron, ductile iron pipes, TMT bars and wire rods, sponge iron (DRI), billets/MS ingots and coke, with intermediate products such as sponge iron and pig iron feeding downstream production or being sold into merchant markets depending on realisations. It sells business-to-business to large OEMs including automotive and construction OEMs and project customers, and business-to-government to government organisations and public sector undertakings, notably supplying DI pipes into flagship water programmes such as the Jal Jeevan Mission and AMRUT. During the year the Company expanded its portfolio by entering the business of OPVC pipes, tubes and fittings.
business.title: What they do

business.body:
- **Ferro alloys:** Specialised ferro alloys, Niche and higher-value alloy grades
- **Ductile iron pipes:** Ductile iron pipes with advanced coating systems for water transmission and distribution
- **Pig iron:** Steel-grade pig iron, Foundry-grade pig iron
- **TMT bars and wire rods:** Scientifically designed TMT bars, Wire rods
- **Sponge iron (DRI):** Direct reduced iron / sponge iron
- **Billets and ingots:** Billets, MS ingots
- **Coke:** Coke, Coke fines, Nut coke
- **Polymer pipes:** OPVC pipes, tubes and fittings (new business entered)

outlook.body: 6-7 months for DI pipes; stable pricing due to long-term contracts; no price erosion expected; order book backed by Jal Jeevan Mission, AMRUT-2, and EPC partners
outlook.title: Order book & pipeline

outlook.body: Export market penetration for DI pipes (currently constrained by domestic demand); potential for specialty ferro alloy exports to 42 countries; captive power plant integration (35TPH waste heat boiler) to reduce grid dependence; future capacity expansion beyond 6.6lakh tons DI and 1.9lakh tons ferro alloys post-FY26
outlook.title: Growth verticals / optionality

outlook.body:
- Jai Balaji 2.0 transformation agenda: build a larger, more integrated, more value-added and financially resilient manufacturing enterprise by progressively increasing the contribution of specialised products, strengthening manufacturing infrastructure, improving operating efficiencies, lowering the cost base and creating greater operating leverage as capacities scale.
- Move from volume to value: shift the portfolio towards DI pipes and specialised ferro alloys where technical capability, product specification and application requirements create differentiation, in order to reduce earnings sensitivity to the commodity cycle rather than to eliminate cyclicality.
- Use vertical integration as the principal hedge: participate across multiple stages of the value chain to retain control over critical inputs, production processes and costs, so margin pressure in a downturn can be managed through internal optimisation, product-mix flexibility and raw-material control.
- Capacity optimisation and phased expansion: continue to scale capacities in a phased manner aligned with projected demand growth while improving asset utilisation and cost efficiency, continuing to invest through the cycle rather than postponing during weak markets.
- Product diversification into high-grade and value-added steel products catering to automotive, defence, renewables and construction equipment.
- Technological advancement: adopt automation and digital technologies and invest in advanced manufacturing processes to enhance operational efficiency, reduce costs and improve product quality and competitiveness.
- Sustainability focus: expand steel recycling by increasing scrap collection networks, upgrading processing plants and adding electric arc furnace capacity, to lower production costs and carbon emissions and reduce dependence on iron ore and coking coal.
- Collaborations and R&D: form strategic alliances with technology providers, research institutions and startups to support innovation in sustainable steelmaking and process optimisation.
- Continued deleveraging and financial discipline alongside investment, optimising borrowing costs by reducing high-cost debt and negotiating lower interest rates, while funding a meaningful part of the next phase of expansion from internally generated accruals.
- Enter and scale the OPVC pipes, tubes and fittings business to leverage synergies with the existing product portfolio and explore new growth opportunities.
- Maintain a safety-first culture across operations as a precondition for sustainable growth.
outlook.title: Strategy & capital allocation

outlook.body: FY 2025-26 was not a year of postponement: management states it continued to advance its long-term capacity expansion programme despite near-term market challenges, on the rationale that scale creates economies of scale, integration improves cost competitiveness, larger capacities create operating leverage and a broader product portfolio gives greater flexibility to respond to changing demand. The Company operates five manufacturing units across West Bengal and Chhattisgarh, supported by captive power and three dedicated railway sidings; the BRSR reports 5 plants and 6 offices nationally plus 1 international office. Two brownfield expansions at existing sites were progressed through environmental impact assessment during the year: a proposed expansion cum modification of the existing steel plant by capacity enhancement at Unit 1 (EIA notification S.O 1533(E) of 14 Sep 2006 and amendments, dated 30 December 2025) and an expansion cum modification of the existing steel plant at Unit 3 (same notification, dated 10 January 2026), both conducted by an independent external agency with results communicated in the public domain on the Parivesh portal. The BRSR confirms these expansion initiatives pertained to brownfield projects at existing locations and did not require a Social Impact Assessment. The Company also expanded its portfolio by entering the business of OPVC pipes, tubes and fittings, intended to leverage synergies with the existing product portfolio. Stated forward intent is to continue scaling capacities in a phased manner aligned with projected demand growth while improving asset utilisation and cost efficiency, to expand steel recycling including additional electric arc furnace capacity, and to fund a meaningful part of the next phase of expansion from internally generated cash flows. No commissioning dates, project capacities or rupee project costs are disclosed in the bundle.
outlook.title: Capex & expansion plans

outlook.body:
- Indian steel demand is expected to rise by around 9% in the next fiscal year, driven by robust infrastructure development, construction activity and expanding manufacturing.
- Government programmes including the National Infrastructure Pipeline, PM Gati Shakti, Smart Cities Mission, Jal Jeevan Mission and increased railway and road investments continue to drive demand for steel and allied products.
- Water infrastructure is described as a multi-year national imperative covering rural drinking-water network expansion, urban modernisation, irrigation investment and replacement of ageing supply networks, backstopped by Jal Jeevan Mission 2.0, AMRUT 2.0 and river-interlinking projects; management believes the difficult phase for the DI pipe industry may represent the lower end of the present demand cycle.
- DI pipe demand in the near term is constrained by the pace of government tendering, funding availability and project implementation; delays during FY 2025-26 reduced demand visibility, constrained capacity utilisation and intensified pricing competition.
- Specialised ferro alloys are a key driver of growth, contributing around 30% of revenues in FY 2025-26, supported by a specialised product portfolio, long-term customer relationships and premium realisations.
- Pricing pressure from global trade imbalances, subdued international steel prices and low-priced imports, particularly from China, continues to weigh on domestic realisations.
- Indian steelmaking capacity rose to 200.33 MT in FY26 and is expected to reach 300 MT by FY30, with secondary producers including MSMEs accounting for nearly 47% of crude steel capacity.
- The Indian ductile iron pipe market is growing steadily on rapid urbanisation, expanding infrastructure and government investment in sanitation and water projects, with DI pipes preferred for their long lifespan and recyclability.
- Growth in the automotive sector, including the shift to electric vehicles, is expected to raise demand for high-quality and specialised steel products.
- Management expects scale economies, deeper integration, higher value addition, a stronger balance sheet and internally generated cash flows to reinforce one another into a virtuous cycle, with internal accruals funding a meaningful part of the next phase of expansion.
outlook.title: Demand & outlook drivers

deepdive.thesis: Jai Balaji is executing a high-ROE transformation via vertical integration, expanding DI pipe and ferro alloy capacity to 80% of revenue mix, while aggressively reducing net debt to zero within 12 months using internal accruals. Strong demand from Jal Jeevan Mission and AMRUT-2, coupled with cost advantages from captive sinter and power, supports sustained EBITDA margins of 18-20%.

sk.overview: India is the world's second-largest crude steel producer and second-largest stainless-steel consumer/third-largest producer, with estimated installed SS capacity of 6.6-6.8 Mn tons. Stainless steel is a high-alloy, corrosion-resistant value-added steel (>10.5% chromium) used across railways, process industries, kitchenware, automotive, construction and infrastructure. Long and flat steel demand is closely tied to overall economic, industrial and consumer activity; the sector is raw-material (SS scrap, nickel, chromium) and energy intensive and prices are volatile.
